opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it came down to scale and focus. In academia, you have a lot of freedom to explore ideas, and that's wonderful. I learned a huge amount from my PhD work. But robotics, especially the kind of general-purpose robot learning we care about, has become very resource-intensive. You need a lot of robots, a lot of diverse data, serious compute, and a strong engineering team to keep everything running reliably. In a typical university lab, it's very hard to put all of those together at the level the problem now seems to require.

At Physical Intelligence, the bet is that a foundation model approach can work for robotics, the way it did for language and vision. Testing that bet properly means collecting data across many different robot embodiments and tasks, and training large models on it. That's not something one grad student or even one lab can easily do. At Pi, researchers, engineers, and operators all work toward the same goal, so ideas get tested quickly and at real scale.

The other thing is the people. Many of my collaborators and people I deeply respect in the field were there. The research culture still feels quite academic in spirit. We publish, we share models, we care about understanding why things work. So it didn't feel like giving up research for a product. It felt like a place to do the research I wanted to do with tools I couldn't get elsewhere.

And to be honest, there's a sense of timing. It feels like a special moment for robot learning, and I wanted to be somewhere I could push hard on the core questions right now, not five years later.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came down to where the real bottleneck in robotics was going to get solved. For years I'd been in a setting where the loop was: have an idea, build a small demo, write the paper, move on. Each paper looked like progress, but the systems were brittle. You'd show a robot folding a towel in one lab, and it couldn't fold a towel in the next building over.

What I came to believe is that robot learning is going to follow the path language and vision took. The breakthroughs won't come from a cleverer architecture on a small dataset. They'll come from scale: huge amounts of diverse real-world data, large models, and the engineering discipline to actually train and deploy them. And that's precisely what academia struggles with. A PhD student can't spend eighteen months building a data collection operation across dozens of robot platforms. The incentive structure doesn't reward it, and the budget isn't there. Pi was built around exactly that bet.

The second thing was the people. At Pi, I'm working with folks like Sergey, Chelsea, Karol, who I knew from research, but now we're all pointed at one problem rather than each defending our own research agenda. That kind of focus is rare. In a university, collaboration across groups is possible but slow. Here it's the default.

And I'd add one more honest reason. I wanted to see things work in the real world, not just in a video attached to a paper. There's a different kind of satisfaction when a policy generalizes to a kitchen no one on the team has ever been in. That feedback from reality is the most valuable research signal I know of, and a company that ships models gets it much faster than a lab does.

I don't think academia is worse. It's still the best place for some questions, especially the weird, long-horizon ones nobody will fund. But for the specific question of whether general-purpose robot foundation models are possible, I think the answer will come from a place with Pi's resources and intensity. I wanted to be where that answer gets found.

astra-6.text:
For me, the attraction was the opportunity to bring ambitious research and real-world robotics much closer together. In robotics, you can have a compelling idea, but you learn something very different when you try to make it work reliably on a physical system. That requires a tight loop between research, engineering, and experimentation.

Academia gives you a lot of freedom to explore, and I value that. What attracted me to Pi was the chance to pursue those fundamental questions with a team focused on making the whole system work. That felt like an exciting environment to push toward more general robot capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the attraction was the chance to bring research and real-world robotics much closer together. In academia, you have a lot of freedom to explore ideas, which is incredibly valuable. But with robotics, you also need the hardware, the data, and the engineering effort to find out whether those ideas actually work outside a controlled setting.

What appealed to me about Pi was the opportunity to pursue fundamental questions while working toward a system that can do useful things. Those goals reinforce each other: trying to make a robot work in the real world exposes gaps in our understanding, and those gaps become the next research questions. That’s a very exciting way to do research.
